UNDERSTANDING STUDENT GROWTH

 Damian W Betebenner
 National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
 Hartford, CT April 28th, 2016

Why Student Growth?

If you care about student achievement,
 then you care about student growth.

๏ Where you are is a function of where you
 started and how quickly you’ve travelled since.
๏ Student growth and student attainment/
 achievement are related in this way.
๏ Distance=Rate x Time
๏ Those who start behind tend to stay behind and
 those that start ahead tend to stay ahead.

“If you can’t solve a problem, then there is an
 easier problem you can solve: find it.”

 George Pólya
Mathematical Discovery on Understanding, Learning, and Teaching Problem Solving, Volume I

A 5th Grade Story Problem

๏ Whose high jump changed more? Explain
 your answer.
๏ Whose high jump change is more
 remarkable? Explain your answer.
๏ Which high jumper improved more?
 Explain your answer.

A 5th Grade Story Problem

๏ Judy improved 2 inches.
๏ Anna Improved 6 inches.
๏ 6 inches > 2 inches.
๏ An inch is an inch!!!
๏ But is an inch really an inch???

A 5th Grade Story Problem

๏ Are we comparing apples to apples?
๏ Anna’s “beginner’s gains” happen in many
 sports.
๏ 2 inches for an elite jumper is far more
 remarkable than 6 inches for a novice.

A 5th Grade Story Problem
 Properties that don’t hold in simple situations will not hold in
 complicated situations. This simple example illustrates how minimally
 helpful a scale is to understanding change.

๏ A vertical scale allows one to answer a
 very narrow question: Who changed
 more?
๏ Remarkable improvement need not be
 synonymous with a large change.
๏ This example illustrates that a vertical
 scale is of little help in answering
 substantive questions.

Another Story
๏ Suppose your child showed no change in height between the ages of 3 and 5.
๏ Upon discovering this your pediatrician responds:

 “Don’t worry, my height
 hasn’t changed for the last 10 years
 and I’m perfectly healthy.”

๏ What do you think of this Doctor’s diagnosis?
๏ Again, 0 inches = 0 inches. But is an inch an inch???
๏ It’s remarkable (and extremely concerning!) for a toddler not to grow. It’s not
 remarkable for an adult to show no change in height.
๏ Context matters!

Student Academic Growth
 ๏ The same holds true for the vertically scaled tests (e.g., SBAC, STAR).

 ๏ Just as an inch isn’t necessarily an inch; a scale score point isn’t

Moral of the Story

Subtraction isn’t a growth model.

 You have to go beyond
 subtraction to understand
 student academic growth.

So how can one
 understand
student growth?

Context is Important
 ๏ Analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
 ๏ Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
 ๏ Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire
 that context.

 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age and is shown to
 have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of increase—4 inches—is a well
 understood quantity that any parent can grasp and calculate at home using a
 simple yardstick. However, parents leaving their pediatrician’s office knowing
 only how much their child has grown would likely be wanting for more
information: Parents are not interested in an absolute magnitude of growth, but
 instead in a norm-referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase alongside
 the height increases of similar children.

Context is Important
๏ Peer-based analyses are sometimes called norm-referenced analyses.
๏ Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are infants/toddlers with
 similar characteristics (e.g., sex and age).
๏ For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are students
 with (at least) the same scale score history on the same tests.
 ๏ Multiple priors give more accurate starting point.
 ๏ Demographics not used but could be.
๏ For interim assessments like STAR, time elapsed between tests is a
 peer characteristic.
๏ Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for
 stakeholders to understand student growth.
๏ Student growth percentiles (SGP) were created to provide a peer-
 based context to understand student academic growth.

Student Growth Percentiles
๏ Research on the SGP model began in 2007 (Betebenner, 2008).
๏ Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced model was extended to
 include a criterion-referenced component. (Betebenner, 2009).
๏ Work in other states incorporating the model into state reporting and
 accountability systems occurred in subsequent years and student growth became
 more common across state assessment systems. (Betebenner, 2012).
๏ Used in approximately 30 states for various diagnostic and accountability
 purposes.
๏ Extended for use with interim assessments in collaboration with Renaissance
 Learning (2015).

Student Growth Percentiles (SGPs)
๏ Similar to height and weight percentiles for infants/toddlers, SGPs range from 1 to
 99.
๏ 1st percentile growth is impoverished and 99th percentile growth is exemplary.
๏ Peer-based growth calculations (SGPs) are only as good as the assessments on
 which they are based.
๏ SGPs are uncorrelated with students beginning level of achievement and allow for
 all students to demonstrate growth regardless of whether they are low or high
 achieving.
๏ SGPs can be aggregated for any group of interest to see whether the group is
 demonstrating, on average, high or low growth.
 ๏ School/District
 ๏ Demographic subgroup
 ๏ Classroom/Teacher
 ๏ Curriculum/Program

Student Growth Percentiles
๏ Peer based comparisons (norms) are helpful but limited by their
 very nature.
๏ Norms tell you where you are in a distribution but not whether the
 ranking is good or bad.
๏ One needs criteria as well as norms to have a complete
 understanding.
๏ A criterion-referenced interpretation examines the quantity against
 a set of standards.
๏ A criterion-referenced interpretation tries to answer:
 ๏ What is “good” growth?
 ๏ What is “bad” growth?
 ๏ What is “good enough” growth?

Student Growth Percentiles
๏ Criterion-referenced growth is also referred to as growth-to-standard.
๏ The standards used to examine growth are often the state’s performance
 standards.
๏ Peer based analyses (e.g., SGP) are used in many states as part of growth-to-
 standard analyses.
๏ Growth-to-standard analyses produce growth targets determining whether a
 student’s growth is sufficient to reach/maintain state standards.
๏ STAR interim assessments also provide growth to standard information where
 the standards are state standards linked to the STAR scale.
๏ Absent norms, criterion-referenced growth produces results similar to
 achievement indicating:
 ๏ Students that start behind tend to stay behind.
 ๏ Students that start ahead tend to stay ahead.

Growth & Accountability
๏ Most of the controversy surrounding student growth analyses centers
 on their (high stakes) uses:
 ๏ Teacher evaluation
 ๏ School evaluation/accreditation
 ๏ Principal evaluation

๏ There is broad disagreement on whether results derived from large
 scale standardized assessments (state summative, interim) are
 appropriate for personnel or institutional evaluation.
๏ Indicators/measures and uses often get conflated leading to push back
 against the measures (assessments) themselves.
๏ There are many great uses for student growth results (SGPs) besides
 personnel/institutional evaluation.

Growth & Accountability
 Non-Accountability Uses of Growth

๏ Progress monitoring of individual students: Is a student on track to
 college readiness?
๏ Curricula evaluation: Do students receiving different curricula
 demonstrate different growth?
๏ Ed-System evaluation: Do students at different grade levels in the
 district grow at the same rate?
๏ Test monitoring: Is their a mode effect in the test administration?
๏ Monitoring progress during standards transition: Were some schools
 more successful at transition to new standards than other schools in
 terms of the growth shown?

Growth & Teacher Evaluation
๏ Likely the most controversial use of tests scores.
๏ Began with Tennessee Value-Added Assessment System (TVAAS now
 EVAAS) in early 90s.
๏ With the availability of longitudinal student assessment data from
 NCLB, data was available in every state for the purpose.
๏ Increased dramatically in late 2000s/early 2010s under Obama/
 Duncan Accountability Policy.
๏ Numerous states also adopted laws requiring teacher evaluation
 based in some part on test scores.
๏ Might have been the straw (along with Common Core) that broke
 the “Ed Reform” back.

Growth & Teacher Evaluation
 Argument #1 for Teacher Evaluation

๏ Value-added methods (VAMs) measure the teacher’s contribution to
 student learning.
๏ Because student learning is important and we can measure the
 teacher’s contribution to it, teachers should be held accountable for
 student learning.
๏ This argument is often proffered by economists.
๏ Arguments against it often focus on the technical characteristics of the
 VAMs:
 ๏ Unreliability: Values can change a lot from year-to-year
 ๏ Invalidity: Examples abound of great teachers receiving low VAM scores.

 ๏ Campbell’s Law: “The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social
 decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the
 more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to
 monitor.”

Growth & Teacher Evaluation
 Argument #2 for Teacher Evaluation
๏ Student learning is important.
๏ Because student learning is important, providers of education should
 be held accountable, in part, for student learning.
๏ Indicators of student learning can be derived from assessment scores
 (e.g., SGP).
๏ Similar to holding a sports coach responsible, in part, for the win/loss
 percentage of his/her team.
๏ Arguments against it often focus on the technical characteristics of the
 VAMs:
 ๏ Unreliability: Values can change a lot from year-to-year.
 ๏ Invalidity: Examples abound of great teachers receiving low growth scores.
 ๏ Campbell’s Law (what often happens when winning is valued too much?)

Growth & Teacher Evaluation

๏ Student growth is usually only a minority part of the overall teacher
 evaluation.
๏ Weights applied to student growth in teacher evaluation vary widely
 (e.g., not at all to 50%).
๏ ESSA has decreased pressure for new teacher evaluation systems in
 states.
๏ Evaluation in non-tested grades/subjects has yielded some
 questionable practices.
๏ Unintended consequences (e.g., Atlanta cheating scandal) provide
 cautionary tales.
๏ What might Accountability 2.0 look like?

Accountability 2.0

๏ Based upon general dissatisfaction with accountability systems
 emerging from the NCLB/Waiver era and new flexibility under ESSA,
 states are asking what an accountability system might look like.
๏ Design principles:
 ๏ Accountability done With stakeholders instead of To
 stakeholders.
 ๏ Accountability as a flashlight instead of a hammer.
 ๏ Data used for improvement instead of punishment.
๏ The change from Accountability 1.0 to 2.0 is more cultural than
 technical.
